catalog_quote: In the default case, the leftmost lexical stress surfaces on a verb. Roots are canonically CVC closed syllables, and moreover may be either weak or strong, such that word-level stress may fall on a functional suffix (Thompson and Thompson 1992). Narrowly focused DPs, on the other hand, are nouns. In the present data set, a large number of these are loan words from English; ... this fact means that stress often falls on an open syllable in the narrowly focused nouns in the present study. In addition, stress always falls on lexical content rather than a functional suffix. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically/morphologically governed rather than positional: roots are lexically 'strong' or 'weak'; a strong root keeps the stress, while with a weak root the stress falls on a (strong) suffix, including lexical suffixes such as =éyus 'pants' or =(m)éix 'house'. Koch attributes the strong/weak root analysis to Thompson & Thompson 1992, whose own formulation (with the full suffix hierarchy) was not opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the opened sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress does not shift under narrow focus: a focused unstressed root (keʔɬ- 'three') stays unstressed while the lexical suffix =éyus 'pants' keeps the word stress; a focused unstressed lexical suffix (=kst 'hand') does not attract stress from the stressed root ləx-lix. English loan nouns (Péter, tiy 'tea') stress the lexical content, often an open syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word-level stress marked with acute accent in T&T orthography); Koch's own study concerns phrase-level nuclear stress, which he finds rightmost in the clause. Koch's data are from two speakers of the Lytton (ƛ'q'əmcín) dialect; the phonemic description he adopts (T&T 1992) is based on the Spuzzum dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Nɬeʔkepmxcín (Thompson River Salish) = thom1243. Koch 2008 data come from the Lytton (ƛ'q'əmcín) dialect; Thompson & Thompson 1992, the description Koch relies on, is based on the Spuzzum dialect. No separate Glottolog dialect codes assigned here.

sources.note: Word-level stress not the topic, but stated in passing: roots are canonically CVC and 'may be either weak or strong, such that word-level stress may fall on a functional suffix (Thompson and Thompson 1992)' (p. 166); examples show stress on a lexical suffix (=éyus 'pants', =(m)éix 'house') with an unstressed root, and stressed roots with unstressed suffixes (pp. 76-77, 96, ~256-258); quotes T&T 1992:21 on stress as a complex of loudness, force and pitch (p. 101); nuclear (phrasal) stress is rightmost in the clause (ch. 4); T&T 1992:24 'phrase-end melodies' summarized p. 35.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2 'Stress and nuclear stress': 'At first glance, Nɬeʔkepmxcin is a classic stress system'; quotes Thompson & Thompson 1992:21 (stress 'a complex of loudness, force, and pitch differences, rather similar in type to the phonetic reality of English stress') and Egesdal 1984:109 ('stress-timed language'); nuclear stress rightmost in the clause. No word-level placement rule given.
